Recent research involving hyperbolic multiple zeta values and generalizations of Apéry's constant has been expanded, including non-linear non-rational multiple zeta values with both odd and even indices. This research was built upon previous findings that established key relationships between these values and an newly developed, broader class of series. Notably, these values are connected to colored multiple zeta functions and their absolute values correspond to 3-apéry numbers, the coefficients of the generating function for the number of 3-colorings of a hexagon. This paper, a continuation of the previous research, focuses on new series similar to those discovered by Apéry, featuring both odd and even summation indices, which will enable us to derive additional identities involving 3-apéry numbers and the values of hyperbolic multiple zeta values. Our analysis is grounded in the method of residue calculation for a specific function of the Riemann type and will provide a framework for understanding the properties of these values and their applications.

Recent data from the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope have allowed us to update the properties of the brown dwarf, WISEA J153429.75-104303.3,, also referred to as "The Mishap". This object, which has a mass similar to that of a brown dwarf, has been estimated to have a age of 830 million years, although this figure is subject to debate. It has been noted that "The Mishap" has a peculiarly low rotation speed, which has allowed it to be used as a test case for theoretical brown dwarf models. This brown dwarf, which has been extensively studied, has been noted to have a relatively large error margin for its mass, which has been found to be 0.06000000000000001 times the mass of the sun, with a confidence level of 95 percent. This work, therefore,, seeks to seek a theoretical explanation for the observed peculiarities in "The Mishap" by examining various theoretical models of brown dwarf models.

A study of the production of various light particles including pions, kaons, proton, anti-proton and phi mesons was conducted in Xe-Xe collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}} = 事件. The measured transverse spectra and initial energy density were compared with calculations from hydrodynamics and a transport model, and the results were also compared to Xe-U collisions at a higher energy of 4.51 TeV per nucleon pair. The data was consistent with expectations of a strongly interacting substance with properties closely matched to those of another known substance.

A novel approach is proposed to determine the x-dependence of parton distribution functions at higher Q^2 scales, by incorporating x-dependence into the DGLAP evolution equations at leading order. The proposed method includes an analytical solution for x^alpha(1-x)^{beta} (x=x_B) functions at the end, with the possibility of expanding on this solution in the future to next-to-leading order as well. The accuracy of the solution is thoroughly examined at the x-values that are relevant to the JLab, LHC, and Tevatron x-values ranges.

In-situ construction on other celestial bodies like the Moon and Mars could be facilitated by using local regolith as building material, if structures can be made by heating and compressing the material, a process known as sintering. To optimize this method, researchers need to understand how to achieve desirable material properties by controlling the process and identifying suitable raw materials, including evaluating regolith from Mars and the Moon. A study was conducted to explore how sintering affects compacts made from Martian and Lunar soil by changing sintering temperatures, and investigating their microstructural and mechanical properties. Results revealed that adding binding agents and increasing pressure led to higher strength in compacts, and that sintering at 300°C or higher created grain bonding and reduced porosity, but only at 600°C did sintering produce optimal mechanical properties for both types of compacts. This study found that using regolith from Mars and the Moon as raw materials could yield strong and durable building materials through sintering, and that understanding how sintering affects material properties is essential for developing effective manufacturing processes for extraterrestrial building materials.

The dynamics of a liquid layer forming on a fiber, suspended in the air, are influenced in the late stage by gravity, surface tension, and slip at the interface with the fiber. A theoretical model describes this process within the framework of the long-wave approximation. This approach is validated by numerical simulations based on the full nonlinear equations of motion. Unlike previous studies that ignored slip and found the diameter of the liquid layer to decrease according to a power law, our findings show that, with a certain level of slip occurring, the transition is changed to an exponential scenario.

We introduce a star formation rate estimator based on the intensity of the Brackett-gamma emission line, determining its luminosity and deriving a star formation rate. By comparing Br$\gamma$ luminosity to star formation rates from Sediment fitting, we find the Br$\gamma$ luminosity to be a reliable indicator of star formation rate, with the relationship described as $L_{\rm br\gamma} = 4.4 \times 10^{12} (S_{8-600})^{1.04}$. This allows us to apply the Br$\gamma$ line to estimate star formation rates in galaxies, with the Br$\gamma$-based rate showing good agreement with rates from other methods, including the far-IR based rate and the H$\alpha$ based rate, for the latter requiring a correction for dust attenuation.

This is the initial paper in a two-part study that explores a type II subquantum group within the sl_N quantum group. To do this, we reframe Tsuchioka's proposed automorphisms of sl_N quantum groups as region-based symmetries acting on the sl_N quantum group central charge k. These transformations can be viewed as Weyl group actions that preserve the sl_N quantum group category, specifically its regional charge and the regional gl_N quantum subgroup. To study this, we develop a new algebraic framework, calling it the 'quantum sub-Weyl algebra', that enables us to characterize these transformations as algebraic operators, including a Bruckner-type multiplication rule.

The diffusion process is a fundamental model used to describe the movement and concentration changes of substances. In this work, an new approach has been developed for solving the general diffusion equation, which can accommodate any type of diffusivity. The proposed method formulates the equation as a nonlinear, first-order system and converts it into an integrable form using a variational matrix. By applying the method of lines with an extrapolation technique for integration, a numerical solution can be obtained. The method's advantages include being a direct, field-based approach that is independent of boundaries. The method's efficiency is highlighted by several example applications, which show that it can provide accurate results with a minimal number of grid points.

This paper outlines an innovative approach to recognizing handwritten mathematical expressions using data obtained from sensors, like those in Graphing Calculator Input Method (GCIM). Graphing input pens with sensor technology can pinpoint the exact location and orientation of written characters by analyzing the input signal they receive. By integrating this precise input data, our model is enhanced and its performance improved. To successfully parse the input data, we developed a custom data transformation that takes into account the sequential order, spatial layout, and specific signal characteristics. This transformed data, called Mathematical Expression Linear Sequence (MELS), serves as the new input for our Convolutional Neural Network (CNN). To validate our method's efficacy, we conducted two experiments, yielding 97.80% and 97.32% accuracy rates respectively.

This paper presents a novel method for generating synthetic speech duration data via the analysis of speech density distributions. Building upon a duration resynthesis system that exploits a speech recognition framework to produce accurate alignments, our approach non-parametrically divides the distribution into segments, calculates the median duration for each segment, and assigns a weighted mean duration. Experimental results using the TIMIT corpus demonstrate that our technique outperforms the traditional minimum variance estimator and a parametric maximum likelihood estimator. Furthermore, the research implicates the significance of incorporating distributions and categorizing data into disjoint intervals in modeling the relationships between acoustic properties and the speech production process.

Conservation analysis and area zoning in ecological studies often require evaluating multiple species simultaneously. A package called spOccupancy facilitates accurate detection of species distributions by accounting for observation errors. This R tool integrates spatial presence models with count data from various sources, such as surveys or capture events, and provides alternative models for different study designs. These models can be used to create management plans, develop policy recommendations, or even conduct maximum entropy analysis. Through simulation studies and real-world examples, spOccupancy demonstrates how to refine decision-making processes in spatial conservation contexts.

The SkinCare initiative is an interactive deep learning system designed to aid dermatologists in diagnosing malignant skin lesions, consisting of two key components: a deep learning network that predicts a patient's skin condition based on an uploaded image, and a multi-class detection system that analyzes an entire patient body to locate all skin conditions. Our deep learning components incorporate advanced techniques such as Data Augmentation, Data Normalization, Data Visualization, and a Data-Driven Network. The proposed system has been evaluated on the ISIC 2017 and 2018 datasets for the medical diagnosis task, achieving state-of-the-art performance with a macro-averaged F1-score of 0.7323 and 0.7610, respectively. For the interactive task, our approach surpassed existing methods by achieving a 10% higher F1-score in identifying melanomas during a dermatology consultation simulation. This work has been accepted for publication as a paper at a computer vision workshop hosted by the International Conference on Medical Imaging and Information Processing in 2019.

To capture the inherent variability in Type Ia supernovae, we employed a probabilistic autoencoder on SNe Ia observations from the ZTF catalog. This approach allowed us to identify a latent space that captures variations in supernovae beyond the two ends of the spectral continuum sub-luminosity range. We found that our approach is more effective in aligning supernovae in the SNe Ia spectral continuum, and we proposed a new approach to derive principal components of supernovae spectra. We found that our approach is more robust in handling noisy spectral data, and we found that the derived latent representations are more coherent and physically meaningful. This approach can be applied to other supernovae subcategories and may provide a new tool for data-driven SNe Ia analysis.

A high-redshift, heavily magnified galaxy, known as CEERS GZK-13, has been discovered. This galaxy, which is located at a redshift of approximately 2.1, features intense light emission from glowing dust and a strong outflow visible in a specific type of light. Although this outflow is visible, it's not fully resolved, which limits our understanding of its properties and the galaxy's starbursts. Researchers have used advanced computer models to create detailed maps of the outflow, even at low spatial resolutions. These models reveal a detailed picture of the outflow, which is now fully resolved for the first time. This new data suggests that the outflow has a speed of around 570 km/s and is composed of two parts moving in opposite directions, which is consistent with previous observations. This new discovery provides valuable information about the outflow's characteristics and the galaxy's starbursts intensity.

A crucial process in geophysical and industrial systems is being explored, which involves the first detailed investigation of flow into particle-laden turbulent plumes. This study provides the first experimental observations of three-dimensional, gravity-affected plumes with suspended particles, using a setup with a modulated flow through a 10 cm oratory and varying particle concentrations up to a value of $N_0=5.5\times10^5$. Video recordings captured the changes in plume morphology and width as a function of height and particle concentration, with theoretical models explaining these effects in terms of turbulent kinetic energy and circulation. Furthermore, our results contradict an earlier assumption that particle-laden regions have the same initial development as particle-free ones, with a critical particle concentration, $N_a$, identified, which marks a transition in plume behavior and depends on the relationship between eddy size and particle settling length, with higher particle concentrations, $N>N_a$, exhibiting a narrower plume and altered flow dynamics, which is being compared to a model with mean flow effects, with varying parameters and different regimes, with resulting effects and different regimes, with resulting effects

Understanding how complex networks evolve over time is essential to grasping various phenomena in hypergraphs, with multiple models proposed to explain this aspect. Here, we derive a condition for extinction in a hyper-SIS epidemic model, where each new infection increases the system's complexity. The model's behavior during an epidemic is closely tied to the spectral properties of a specific matrix, with the given extinction condition relating to its largest eigenvalue. Furthermore, we demonstrate that as the infection rate increases, the epidemic threshold converges to that of a traditional graph-based model. In contrast, with a lower infection rate, the threshold converges to that of a hyper-SIR model, with the latter's parameters adjusted accordingly.

Recent breakthroughs in spintronics have centered on a new class of materials, 2D van der Waals (VdW) ferromagnets. Although exceptionally thin and ferromagnetic in nature, these materials, despite being two-dimensional and ferromagnetic, exhibit unique properties such as chirality, leading to intriguing spin dynamics. Unlike traditional antiferromagnetic systems, chirality in these materials plays a significant role in their spin behavior, an aspect that we've explored in our research. Specifically, we investigated the effects of chirality and Rashba interactions on the spin texture of a 2D CrI3 ferromagnetic system. We discovered that low-energy electron states within this system exhibit a nontrivial spin texture characterized by a in-plane spin component, an attribute that we attribute to a combination of spin-orbit, ferromagnetic, and broken inversion symmetries, all stemming from its chiral properties. Furthermore, we observed that Rashba interactions significantly influence the spin texture, transforming it into a more complex structure with localized spin states, an attribute that we attribute to the presence of a out-of-plane magnetic moment. Our research not only identifies the unique spin properties contained within 2D ferromagnetic systems but also paves the way for their potential application in next-generation spintronics.

By incorporating a rotation profile into mean-field solar-type dynamos, we've discovered that stars with slow rotation rates exhibit magnetic cycles driven by the interaction of rotation and shear. As the rotation rate decreases, the critical magnetic Reynolds number increases, and the mean-field alpha effect is weakened. In contrast, the rotation-based kinetic alpha effect is significantly less impacted, leading to a potential cycle in non-rotating stars. However, the loss of rotational influence also results in a substantial decrease in mean-field shear and the emergence of a baroclinic shear dominant over the rotation-driven elliptical shear. These conditions cause the spectral energy distribution of the dynamo to shift towards higher frequencies, resulting in shorter magnetic cycles. Our findings suggest that kinetic-based and hybrid dynamos with rotation-dependent kinetic alpha effects are better suited to model solar-type magnetic cycles and that the relationship between rotational influence and the spectra of generated spectra is universal, potentially applicable to star formation regions with pervasive magnetic fields.

Deep neural networks are highly effective at processing complex data, but their success depends on addressing a critical challenge: representation learning. Our proposed k-fan deep framework addresses this challenge by efficiently organizing and processing complex data with multiple input types. This innovative framework structures the learning of shared representations for all input types in a highly compact and organized manner, enabling effective handling of high-dimensional data. Through multiple transformation planes, the network filters and separates different data modalities into distinct branches, facilitating efficient learning of modality-specific representations in parallel. Our framework was put to the test on complex data classification and dimensionality reduction tasks, including a novel application on knowledge-based learning with multiple knowledge inputs, and showed promising results in handling complex data.

The use of model verification has become essential for detecting subtle bugs in complex, multi-threaded programs despite their minimal performance impact. In recent, single-core processors, the need for model verification remains equally essential, particularly for accurately reflecting the effects of out-of-order execution and store buffering. This paper presents a new model verifier, McMini, based on dynamic partial order reduction, which is highly adaptable and suitable for detecting store-check and schedule-visibility bugs in C programs using the CBMC tool. By doing so, McMini helps researchers and developers validate existing model verification methods and explore new avenues for verifying multi-threaded programs. Additionally, McMini outperforms a competing model checker, Spin, which utilizes a spinning validation approach, demonstrating superior performance even for programs involving minimal overhead on existing processors.

This paper investigates the effectiveness of restricting forwardable messages on 
WhatsApp's misinformation spread of such a policy to limit information dissemination. 
Our study tracks actual misinformation propagation using a dataset of WhatsApp threads 
containing misinformation and compares the impact of limiting information sharing. 
We also investigate the motivations behind users' decision to share messages and the 
attributes that make them more likely to disseminate them. 
Our analysis shows that while limiting message forwarding does reduce the spread of 
misinformation, it does not necessarily prevent its dissemination, as users' choices are 
also influenced by personal beliefs.

We analyze a broad class of population models, including those with sex, where each generation depends on a random number of individuals from the previous one. These models are assumed to be linear, non-homogeneous branching processes with generally unequal male and female numbers, leading to a non-constant growth rate and a stable, positive long-term population proportion. An important aspect of these models is the emergence of a new long-term distribution of allele frequencies, distinct from previous short-term distributions. This new distribution, however, is difficult to compute directly. To address this challenge, we develop an approximation of this evolutionary frequency distribution using integral methods. Our approach is illustrated through two specific population models: one representing a homogeneous, asexual, positive Markov population and another sex-based, non-homogeneous branching population.

This paper introduces an innovative attentive activation mechanism designed to boost the effectiveness of spoofing detection systems by precisely matching the length of input feature vectors with those of their corresponding channel dimensions. Built upon an neural network architecture that leverages an attention mechanism, this system is ideal for applications where feature vector length flexibility is a constraint. To broaden its scope of use, we developed a downscaling mechanism that is compatible with many downscaling methods. This downscaling mechanism can be integrated into various spoofing detection systems, including those employing a dynamic convolutional layer, an innovative multi-channel mechanism, and a deep bidirectional approach. Our results demonstrate a notable enhancement in spoofing detection performance across a range of datasets including ITI-SPOOF-2019, DERIVATIVES, and SACRE.

We explore the full range of supersymmetric effective field theories describing cosmological inflation. Within this framework, D-term models emerge as a globally supersymmetric subset, with our analysis revealing new models and establishing a mapping between certain EFIs, their non-supersymmetric counterparts, and a specific model featuring an EFIS. Interestingly, we find that T-marginal relations can lead to complex and chaotic supergravity scalar potentials. Consequently, our approach enables the systematic derivation of scalar potentials, ensuring they adhere to theoretical constraints, while our results also include constraints on EFIs derived from the gravitational bootstrap method.

Parametric down-conversion produces correlated photon pairs and is a valuable resource to study and manipulate quantum mechanics. However, theoretical models and experiments have shown that the asymptotic correlation of the photon pairs can be different for the signal and idler photons. This phenomenon, which is different from the more commonly discussed bipartite entanglement, was confirmed through measurements of the von Neumann entropy in the HBT system.

The dynamic behavior of superconducting quantum circuits is an area of active research and development, and it's essential to understand microwave resonances and field distributions. We have created a terahertz Scanning Near-field Microwave Holography system, and it can image microwave resonators at 10 GHz with high precision, comparable to near-field terahertz spectroscopy. By combining a superconducting Meissner effect probe and a superconducting loop, and applying a vector holographic method, our system enables the separate reconstruction of the terahertz field's in-plane and out-of-plane components. We have successfully used this system to characterize field distributions and quality factors of co-planar waveguide microwave resonators, and it may provide a bridge to characterize more complex superconducting quantum circuit systems.

Given an arbitrary partition of the real axis into subsets $X_i$, we investigate Lebesgue measure and nullity of the graphs associated with functions that are absolutely continuous, strictly increasing, and map the reals to the reals. We establish that functions satisfying these criteria will have graphs divided into measurable sets $E_f(x,y)$ by our prescribed partition, where $E_f(x,y)$ contains the values of function pairs. We establish the existence of such functions in an optimal manner for any given partition, particularly focusing on homeomorphisms, and consider specific applications such as Borel sets and partition by the reals line, where countable exceptions are avoided.

In the past few years, a surge in research on utilizing artificial intelligence in trading has been observed, primarily centered around predicting stock prices through advanced machine learning techniques. This rapid development has largely been driven by the potential to generate stock price predictions, yet the underlying methodology has not received sufficient attention. This research delves into the consequences of deploying multiple trading agents, utilizing an established agent-based market model, to simulate the effects of a multitude of co-existing investment tactics on the stock market. Our findings suggest that a diverse group of agents can have a substantial impact on the performance of the market, with outcomes varying based on the tactics' underlying methodology. Notably, we observed that the unanticipated side effects are most pronounced when the majority of agents adhere to a single paradigm, for instance, technical trading strategies.

Identifying network traffic behavior and application protocols is crucial for detecting anomalies, vulnerabilities, and threats in network systems. The problem, however, is exacerbated by anomalous and non-standard traffic patterns that can confuse traditional detection methods, leading many network operators to rely on proprietary, commercial solutions. Despite significant advancements in machine learning and transfer learning, these tools face challenges related to data availability, training time, and the need for specialized expertise, hindering their adoption by security professionals with limited experience. This study reviews state-of-the-art techniques for protocol detection, highlighting their advantages and limitations to provide a foundation for selecting or designing a suitable method. Furthermore, it proposes and evaluates two novel methods - hyperparameter optimization using genetic algorithms and fast nearest neighbor learning - to demonstrate their practical feasibility in a tested and verified DDPID approach.

We investigate how thermal gating affects the flow of thermal and electrical currents in a single magnon channel by using a tunable thermal barrier. A key finding is that both electrical and thermal conductivities can be controlled via the gate in a system consisting of a superconducting plate and a magnetic insulator. Our data reveal that both conductivities exhibit similar temperature-dependent behaviors, which we attribute to a specific zone theory for both electrical and thermal transport. Our results also show that both conductivities can be coherently controlled by varying the gate temperature and provide strong evidence that superconducting gating can enable the development of spin caloritronic devices and superconducting thermoelectric systems based on magnons.

A recent advancement in deep learning, known as federated learning, allows multiple users to collaboratively develop or update DFAs using local data, thus preserving their privacy. The popularity of federated learning has grown in fields like computer vision and healthcare, but it remains underexplored in other areas, such as audio processing. This research extends the concept to include learning DFAs from data with different labels at various federated rounds, known as zero-shot federated learning. Our study focuses on two commonly used audio classification datasets, where we compare novel approaches with existing methods. The results show that by leveraging transferability and ensemble techniques, the performance of the audio classifiers can be enhanced significantly.

There have been multiple methods to measure Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger (GHZ) states in experiments to date, each with its own approach and context. To expand our understanding, we have formulated a general, mathematical framework for GHZ states in any number of dimensions and configurations, applicable to both discrete-variable systems and continuous variables. Our research demonstrates that, in discrete-variable setups, a single complete measurement can achieve the measurement of all GHZ states by employing the Fourier GHZ basis. Similarly, we have found a suitableGHZ basis in all continuous-variable configurations that allows for the measurement of all GHZ states through a single measurement. Our work offers a new theoretical perspective on GHZ states in discrete-variable systems and provides practical guidance for implementing measurements in both discrete-variable and continuous-variable experiments.

This research paper delves into the design of a novel, two-stage cascaded channel estimation method for multi-user multiple-input-single-output systems supported by intelligent reflecting surfaces. The authors propose a novel system architecture in which the single antenna at the BS connects to a solitary node behind the IRS, requiring only a limited number of configurable elements for pilot channel reception. As a result, the overall connectivity matrix can be decomposed into two sub-matrices representing the direct and reflected paths, respectively. While the received signal is initially processed to determine the optimal node placement for maximizing the direct channel's F-norm, these results are then utilized to devise a two-stage estimation method. The authors also present a closed-form expression for the estimation error, providing insight into the trade-off between system complexity and overall connectivity. Furthermore, a low-complexity node allocation strategy based on the least-squares estimator is introduced to minimize the error, resulting in considerable improvements over existing methods, especially under low SNR conditions.

This study provides unique insights into how U.S. local news online reports COVID-19 and its related issues, uncovering a user-friendly data resource for analyzing the media landscape during a global pandemic. Utilizing a user-friendly interface, we identified and examined a broad range of local news outlets, including websites with no, low, or high engagement in COVID-19 reporting, while analyzing their community demographics and pandemic impact statistics. Our findings show that local news outlets initially increased COVID-19 reporting in response to daily deaths, but eventually shifted to more sustained and sustained patterns. Using a significant dataset, the study maps COVID-19 coverage trends, cases, deaths, and audience engagement, revealing nuanced relationships between local news decisions and public health outcomes.

This study investigates the feasibility of neural networks, specifically augmented with recurrency, to model complex tasks such as counting progression. Our research demonstrates that these networks can learn to count with memory when tasks are structured in a way that allows them to anticipate the next step, but the pattern breaks down when the task involves learning from random mistakes. In order to overcome this limitation and enable accurate learning of counting sequences, we propose modifying the loss function, and this adaptation also improves the network's performance in predicting the future based on current states.

Bloom filters provide an approximate method for determining if an element is part of a set at the cost of memory, with false positive rates dependent on allocated memory. They offer a balance of speed and space efficiency. A Cuckoo filter variant can also achieve a similar compromise, generally producing lower error rates, but requiring more memory than Bloom filters. Our research introduces a novel filter called Xor filters that can realize all the useful properties of Bloom and Cuckoo filters while being a constant multiplier (1x) in terms of memory usage and (0.75x) in size efficiency compared to Bloom filters, with a 2-4x reduction in update time, 3-8x reduced deletion time, 3-8x lower error rates, and maintained query speeds. Moreover, Xor filters support partial updates and pre-calculation to enable even faster processing times in our evaluated environments. Ours filters combine the speed and adaptability of Cuckoo filters with the memory efficiency of Bloom filters for a superior alternative.

We establish a connection between semi-norms on vector spaces without norm, 
the support functions of their convex cones, and hyperbolic domains. Specifically, 
we show that a semi-norm gives rise to a convex cone, whose support function can be used 
to define a hyperbolic space. This allows us to prove that every such semi-norm 
corresponds to a complex affine space with a bounded strong convex cone, 
by translating the concepts of conjugate dual and positive homogeneity. 
Additionally, continuous semi-norms correspond to normal families of holomorphic maps, 
while closed cones correspond to Grauert-Stein spaces. Further, we discuss duality 
and its implications for duality in convex geometry, dual semi-norms, and Einstein metrics.

Traditional price-based models of the stock market have long been used for pricing, trading, and forecasting, primarily focusing on daily price changes. Despite the widespread adoption of these models, they have never been validated due to the lack of a standard data representation for the future price changes. To address this gap, we propose a novel data representation for future price changes, enabling an in-depth analysis of past and present market behavior. By calculating the time-weighted correlation of price changes, we develop a statistical test to distinguish the direction of price changes. This approach enables us to investigate the directional data of past and present market behavior, providing insights into the directionality of price changes. Our analysis reveals the existence of weak negative directionality in the S\&P 500 index from 1990 to 2019, as well as varying levels of directionality in individual stocks, with notable buy-then-sell patterns observed. Furthermore, we found that low directionality stocks exhibit higher returns, consistent with the HML factor in the Fama-French model, and our directionality measure correlates with the ILLIQ factor, as low directionality stocks are quicker to adapt and respond to new information.

This paper presents a privacy-preserving FLvoogd protocol, which integrates Federated Averaging, Laplace noise, and a variance-reduction technique to enhance privacy in Federated Learning under constraints of limited communication bandwidth. The FLvoogd protocol is evaluated through both theoretical analysis and empirical tests, showing its communication efficiency and improved accuracy compared to existing privacy-preserving methods while maintaining robust differential privacy guarantees.

Most autonomous vehicle research relies on simulated environments to generate labeled data, but this labeled data often fails to translate to real-world scenarios due to differences in domain. A new approach to transfer this simulated data to reality, beyond simple scaling, is missing from current research. We propose a novel framework that leverages image gradients to align simulated and real-world scenes. This framework fine-tunes an existing autonomous driving model using unsupervised real-world data, effectively bridging the gap between simulation and reality. We tested this framework on the autonomous landing of quadrotors, achieving significant improvements in transferability and simulation-to-real performance.

A real-time generation and detection system for Deepfakes has been developed to counter misinformation spread on social media platforms. The current implementation, however, has limitations, particularly in its reliance on specific media types. To overcome this restriction, this research aims to create an advanced Deepfake generation model that can be applied to any media type, without limitations. The proposed model, along with an improved detection algorithm, will push the boundaries of its feasibility.

The orbits of many large planets around their stars overlap with the Habitable Zone, where temperatures permit liquid water on nearby smaller planets. The detection of smaller planets capable of hosting life-altering conditions is critical for our understanding of the universe. The key to discovering these worlds may lie in the diverse atmospheric compositions of larger gas planets, which could range from water-rich to gas-dominated, depending on the balance between soluble and insolubel components. We present a novel method to analyze these variations, focusing on soluble water and carbon monoxide in particular, and using recent transit spectroscopy data from smaller gas planets GJ 347 b, GJ 1132 b, and K2-18 b, and the exoplanet atmosphere mapper EXASTUS, to explore the solubility balance vs. geochemical balance hypothesis. Our analysis of transmission spectra of these exoplanets suggests that the gases we see are dominated by water and methane and gas and carbon monoxide, and their solid forms, carbon and ice, and the rocks and silicates they sit on. We propose that the excess ice and carbon on these exoplanets could be the missing link in their geological and chemical evolution, and the ultimate source of life on these planets.

Recent studies have demonstrated the capability of Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) to learn sequential tasks, however, increasing the length of sequences typically results in a significant decrease in accuracy, a phenomenon known as the "gradients vanish" issue. In this paper, we investigate whether a Sequentia language model can effectively learn sequential data using a Dynamic Direct Mapping (DDM) method without encountering the "gradients vanish" problem in Neurons based on Long-Term Potentiation/Depression (LTP/LTD) and Short-Term Plasticity (STP). Our research indicates that the DDM method can effectively eliminate the "gradients vanish" problem, provided that a sufficiently large number of neurons is used. Our findings also show that the DDM method is a highly efficient approach for sequence learning, capable of accurately modeling complex, real-world data, such as the C-9 dataset. DDM is a novel architecture that maps each input directly to its corresponding output, thereby eliminating the need for intermediate hidden states. Our investigation has revealed that the DDM method is a highly effective alternative to the standard RNN approach, particularly for long, complex sequences. DDM is a novel architecture that maps each input directly to its corresponding output, thereby eliminating the need for intermediate hidden states. Our investigation has revealed that the DDM method is a highly effective alternative to the standard RNN approach, particularly for long, complex sequences.

This report details the methods and results obtained from participating in out-of-category challenges designed to assess a model's performance on unforeseen categories. Our approach involved a two-stage process: initial domain adaptation to transfer knowledge from known to unknown categories, followed by a detection of the model's limitations and the identification of novel categories. Due to differences in evaluation metrics between challenges, we developed two separate models, each trained for a specific challenge, but found a common bottleneck - confidence of over-85% was consistently assigned to a small set of categories. To address this issue, we implemented re-ranking techniques to more evenly distribute confidence scores across all categories. In the LC03 challenge, we utilized category embeddings to locate the model's nearest neighbors in a high-dimensional space, representing potential novel categories. We introduced two metrics for these neighbors - the distance from the centroid and the diversity of the categories associated with the neighbors. Results indicated that models tended to be confident about neighbors belonging to a limited pool of categories, and performance reached its peak around 15 novel categories before declining. Peak F1 scores of 0.7 achieved at around 7 novel categories represented the model's maximum discovery capacity. Our methods in the LC04 challenge diverged, focusing on identifying categories with low-confidence predictions. We established a threshold of 0.85 for high-confidence predictions and evaluated the remaining predictions using F1 scores, reporting an F1 of 0.5 achieved at 15 low-confidence categories. Additionally
A new approach for assessing the accuracy of Generalized Polynomial Chaos approximations is presented, along with the method's numerical validation across various examples.

This paper develops an innovative adaptive algorithm for detecting and isolating changes in a complex system with incomplete information. Focusing on sequential linear observation models that operate under sparse and distributed constraints, the authors devise a statistical test based on residual analysis to identify when a change occurs and employ a logical inference approach using relative entropy to isolate the anomaly. By combining partial observability, sparsity, and rationality principles, the algorithm efficiently narrows down potential sources of change, making it computationally feasible. After demonstrating its success in identifying changes within artificial data, the authors applied the algorithm to real-world traffic flow data from the I-95 highway to detect variations within the same area at different times and successfully pinpoint the exact location of the changes.

We have created a novel machine learning model using chi-squared minimization to analyze the properties of dwarf galaxies, focusing on their behavior within the cosmological CD98 model. This chi-squared model accounts for key factors, such as the galaxy's present-day mass, number of subunits, and the distribution of mass among those subunits. This is the first time such a model has been applied to literature data, allowing us to extract valuable information about dwarf galaxies. Our analysis of data from dwarf irregular galaxies revealed that they are largely consistent with the predictions of the CD98 model, whereas we found that dwarf spheroidal galaxies deviate from its predictions. This discrepancy may stem from the unique chemical evolution of dwarf spheroidal galaxies, potentially influenced by their dry mergers.

Given a profinite group $G$, an action spectrum is a function $\pi_*(-)^G$, which takes $G$-spectra as input and returns homotopy groups of spectra. This theory builds on existing work by Bergner and Bergner-Madhusudhan for arbitrary topological groups. In our context, continuous cohomology is substituted with continuous etale cohomology. Our approach relies on a model category of profinite $E\mathcal{M}$-spectra, where $\mathcal{M}$ is a site. This is achieved by adapting methods proposed by Bergner and Bergner-Madhusudhan, and the action spectrum is defined as follows: for a $G$-spectrum $X$, $\pi_*(-)^G(X)$ is equal to the homotopy groups of maps in $\mathcal{M}$, where $S$ to $S_G$, where $S_G$ is constructed as the Borel construction of $\mathcal{M}$, $G$, and the profinite topologization of $\mathcal{M}$.

A major challenge with large language models for NLP tasks is obtaining a sufficient amount of labeled training data. Our approach to this issue involves leveraging pre-trained multilingual language models, which we enhance by fine-tuning them on a small set of labels and then using them to generate a large amount of synthetic data. This synthetic data is used to pre-trained models that are commonly fine-tuned for document-based NLP tasks, which we then re-train to produce a strong extraction model. This process, which we term DataAugMENT, can dynamically and extraction-task-specifically augment training data. Our experiments on various document extraction tasks show that DataAugMENT can significantly reduce labeling costs while also improving extraction model performance, especially when a limited amount of labeled data is available. Our findings are as follows: it can reduce labeling costs by up to 5 times without a decline in model performance; it can even surpass models trained on fully labeled data; and it outperforms current state-of-the-art approaches in various document extraction tasks.

The EuS/InAs interface has garnered significant interest due to its potential to display quantum anomalous Hall effect. The hall effect may arise from the magnetic bound states near the EuS/InAs interface, which results from the magnetic ordering in the EuS layer. The linking configuration at the EuS/InAs interface has a significant impact on the system's magnetic properties. The first-principles calculations were performed to investigate the electronic structure and magnetic properties of different EuS/InAs linking configurations. By comparing these linking configurations, it has been determined that they significantly affect the bound states within the InAs band gap, which in turn influence the topological properties of the system. Specifically, it has been found that the band gap in the InAs material is partially occupied in some of these configurations, making the system quantum Hall active. The quantum hall active linking configuration exhibits a chiral edge state at the EuS/InAs interface, which topologically separates the bulk InAs. The results of this study may provide a basis for the design and implementation of topological magnetic devices.
A detailed classification of Borel wadge classes is provided, featuring an arbitrary number of levels.

High-precision deep learning model training requires expensive HPC systems,
but recent advances in inference-focused pruning have not kept pace with
potential improvements in training. Our work, ClickTrain, fills this gap by
creating the first training-oriented fine-grained pruning method, designed to
be flexible and efficient. ClickTrain achieves a bandwidth reduction of up to
5x during knowledge distillation and a up to 2.5x reduction in memory usage
during P2P communication and gradient computation, all while maintaining high
accuracy. It's compatible with existing frameworks and achieves a training speedup
of nearly two-fold. ClickTrain can be applied to various network architectures
and a wide range of tasks, offering significant benefits in resource
utilization without compromising model accuracy.

It's widely acknowledged that the distribution law is missing from nonassociative modal logic's Lambek calculi, particularly in its simpler forms like the Lambek Calculus with Identity (PCI) and its complex variant, the Type Theory (PTT). This paper identifies a specific subset of formulas in PCI and PTT that contain a implicit form of distribution, showing that each formula's validity implies a total order structure on the language's alphabet, which can be used to define a complete, lambda calculus-based system for each theory.

The diverse and evolving nature of electromagnetic and gravitational waves from merging neutron star-black hole systems offers a unique window into the dynamics of extreme gravity sources. Although current detectors can observe gravitational waves, the vast range of masses involved limits their chi-squared parameter. To overcome this, a convolutional neural network was trained to analyze real detector data, accurately identifying and characterizing NSBH coalescences. When trained on parameters within a specific mass range, the model demonstrated a 99% efficiency in detecting gravitational waves and distinguishing them from detector noise, but its performance declined with coalescence parameters outside its training parametric space, underscoring the significance of artificial horizon in the phase transition.

A comprehensive study of the exoplanet TOI-5542 has been conducted, including its host star and its co-orbiting gas giant, utilizing archival and new data sources. The exoplanet TOI-5542 b is a warm Jupiter with approximate dimensions of 1.15 times that of Jupiter, residing in a low-metallic environment with a 99.98% probability of being a true gas giant at an orbital distance of around 0.25 AU. Its discovery, driven by a combination of transit and radial velocity data, is consistent with both models and theories of giant planet migration through the TOI-5542's protoplanetary disk. Due to TOI-5542's distant location in the galaxy, it's posited as a prime candidate for simulating the photometric signatures of giant planets in galaxy-like settings, simulating Hubble's observations of the exoplanet Jupiter. The data of TOI-5542 has now been integrated with existing exoplanet data sets to investigate patterns of giant planet properties across various metallicities in their galaxies.

A constrained Markov decision process (CMDPC) is an optimization framework that incorporates resource constraints into stochastic decision-making processes. It seeks to identify a strategy that maximizes expected rewards while minimizing expected costs under uncertainty. CMDPCs effectively model complex, constrained decision-making scenarios in diverse fields, including robotics, economics, and operations research. They underpin decision-making systems that balance performance and resource consumption in complex, dynamic environments. This paper explores a primal-dual algorithm to solve the linear programming formulation of CMDPCs. We analyze the algorithm's convergence and provide theoretical guarantees for its convergence rate. Our results compare the algorithm to existing methods and highlight its competitive performance. Finally, we validate the algorithm's efficacy through numerical experiments on synthetic and real-world problems.

This research presents an advanced offline handwritten mathematical expression recognition system, which uses deep learning techniques. The system incorporates modified Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) for encoding and decoding sequences, which are modified to incorporate sequence-based features and utilize hidden state for contextual information. The outcome of this advanced encoding is fed into a Transition-based Recurrent Neural Network (TRNN) that integrates multi-object detection and parsing capabilities. This research also compares the effects of different image extraction techniques on recognition performance, demonstrating that our system outperforms existing systems, especially when using vector quantization and occlusion detection techniques, which yield state-of-the-art results.

A key finding in previous research connects the first cohomology of a Riemann surface to the spectrum of supercharges in supersymmetric quantum particles. Expanding on this, the present paper investigates how the Betti numbers of cohomology groups on a compact Kähler manifold relate to the cohomological dimension, which is defined as the maximum value of b_p.

To analyze the irregular fluctuations in events occurring on network components, we employ a probability distribution and investigate its components using a network model. Our analysis demonstrates that parts of this distribution can be effectively represented by both its mean and variance, whereas other parts exhibit greater complexity and depend on the structure of the network and properties of connections.

Recently, a novel method, the actor-critic reinforcement learning algorithm, has become a popular choice for solving Markov decision processes. Although it has achieved significant success in reinforcement learning, it can become trapped in local optima when processing high-dimensional continuous problems. To address this limitation, a new method, a Hamiltonian Monte Carlo method, has been proposed to improve the efficiency of the actor-critic algorithm in such scenarios. By guiding policy gradients along Hamiltonian trajectories, this method increases the probability of escaping local optima and explores the solution space more effectively. The proposed method, a Hamiltonian Monte Carlo method, can be integrated with various actor-critic algorithms, including those based on trust regions. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of this method in solving continuous reinforcement learning tasks.

Basic number theory knowledge is used to demonstrate that in any sequence of k consecutive even numbers, at least two numbers share the same prime factorization with k + 1 or more prime factors, leading to the conclusion that in sufficiently large enough values of k, there are two numbers with k + 1 or more prime factors that differ by a small even number.

Achieving precise and agile manipulation outside of clean laboratory settings is a significant challenge for robots. The complex environment is characterized by a high error rate and its dynamic nature, particularly with objects having irregular shapes. Our research focuses on leveraging sonar technology to track close-range spatial states of a specific class of robots - those employing layered navigation controllers - to enhance their navigation capabilities. This integration involves introducing a sonar-based alert system to supplement existing visual navigation, allowing the robot to navigate around unmodeled obstacles in real-time. Our study evaluated the robustness of this Sonar Integration (SI) in a robot with layered navigation, demonstrating its ability to leverage sonar data for real-time spatial state estimation. This technology has now been applied to a mobile manipulator to facilitate safe navigation in close proximity to humans in clinical settings, where human safety is a top priority.

The discovery of complex organic molecules (tholins) on Neptune's moons Nereid and Nereida has raised questions about their formation. Recent models suggesting a photochemical process for these compounds have raised concerns regarding the production of light-colored minerals like kaolinite and quartz, which would not be generated in sufficient quantities. An alternative model proposing thermal processing of water ice to produce both tholins and light-colored minerals is therefore more plausible. We analyzed the reflectance spectra of Nereida to determine the relative amounts of water ice, quartz, and calcium sulfate using a water ice model and endmember mineral mixtures. Our results from a Bayesian analysis indicate that calcium sulfate is present on Nereida at levels of 10-30% and quartz at levels of 10-25%, consistent with thermal processing model. These findings support this model and provide a basis for further investigation into the formation of complex organic compounds on Neptune's moons.

We establish the equivalence of two theorems concerning projective and affine lines over a specific type of matrix ring, which implies the equivalence of the corresponding theorems regarding projective and affine planes. This equivalence can be further broken down into the equivalence of the theorems concerning lines in projective space.

We establish the exact conditions for the Tukey-order relationship between two specific collections of reals, derived from models that satisfy Pawlikowski's fundamental principles. Consider two sets of reals, $\mathbb{R}_1$ and $\mathbb{R}_2$, where the first set contains all reals associated with strong measure or category reals, and the second set contains all reals associated with almost disjoint sets. We determine that the set of reals in the first collection is Tukey-equivalent to the set of reals in the second collection if and only if the set of reals in the first collection contains the set of reals in the second collection. This equivalence can be established through three newly proven theorems, and our results expand upon existing work, and are applicable in a broader context, and are not limited to specific set theories.

This research introduces a new concept called negativity in the context of counterfactual analysis for ITRs, offering a quantitative measure of the distinction between optimal and suboptimal decisions. By formalizing negativity, we determine the minimum cost difference between making an incorrect decision and its consequence, providing a minimum threshold for IT. Negativity is shown to be linked to the regret in counterfactual learning problems, and our findings introduce an efficient algorithm for estimating negativity in certain scenarios. This new measure is particularly useful for assessing the stability and reliability of counterfactual policies, and our work connects negativity to both the risk of model selection and the minimum gap in counterfactual learning.

This note explores connections between different meanings of dual categories to illustrate
some common features between graph dualities and duality theories in topology or logic. 
It also covers duality theories for posets lattices and algebras as well as duality theories for formal concept analysis.

A recently proposed complexification of the $E_8$ core system, an adaptation of the Grinberg-Karevoldi system, is examined here, with a demonstration of its ability to generate a non-contextual hidden variable model for Bell and anti-fermentality non-locality and impossibility proofs. This model's construction relies on quantum entanglement and operator contextuality, providing an understanding of the E8 core system's role in these phenomena. This development is relevant in the study of the role of octonions in quantum physics.

We develop a method to investigate superconductivity in complex systems with multiple interacting particles, employing a specialized representation of the wave function that is particularly effective for superconducting states. This approach is applied to two-dimensional superconductors with both spinless and spinful frustrated Kagome superconductors with superconducting gaps. Our findings reveal a wide range of superconducting phases in these non-Abelian topological insulators, characterized by distinct orders such as chiral, flux-chiral, and loop-order. Furthermore, we identify unique signatures of these phases, including edge currents, corner modes, and flux order, as well as their impact on the responses to external disturbances and quasiparticle responses.

We have proven that if G is a group with the local property, then the free Abelian topological group generated by G is of dimension at most 1 and we have also proven the linked theorem: G is not of dimension 1 if and only if its free group is not of dimension 1. Furthermore, we establish the embedded theorem: if a set A in G is not of dimension 1, then its free group, denoted as F(A), can be mapped onto a set within G that has A as an embedded subset and is also of dimension 1. The exponent group F(A)[p^{\infty}] of F(A) has the property of being a quasicompact, quasilocal, and Abelian topological group, where each open subset in F(A)[p^{\infty}] has a non-empty intersection with A[p^{\infty}], the subgroup in A consisting of the p-elements.

Presence-absence data is commonly collected in ecological studies in a binary format, representing species occurrence. This type of data has become central in ecological research due to its direct relation to essential concepts like species distribution and community structure. Clustering techniques have been utilized to identify concealed patterns within species data. This study compares various clustering methods suitable for high-dimensional presence-absence data, considering both static and time-series time series. To evaluate these methods, we utilized four publicly accessible ecological datasets and assessed their performance using three distinct measures: intra-cluster compactness, inter-cluster separation, and biological relevance. By incorporating an approach that integrates domain expertise, we evaluated each cluster's meaningfulness through the inspection of relevant ecological literature. To identify optimal clustering results, we examined how hyperparameters influence performance. The results revealed that choosing suitable data preprocessors is crucial for achieving satisfactory clustering outcomes, with no single method surpassing others consistently. Similarly, no single clustering method excelled in comparison to others. Conversely, modules C and C2 demonstrated the most reliable performance across different comparisons.

In recent years, salient object detection in both monocular RGB and RGB-D images has been widely studied, with new models being proposed frequently. Although these models achieve high accuracy on images without depth information, they often struggle with images that include depth data. To address this issue, a novel and unified framework is presented here that leverages the unique properties of both RGB and depth information in both training and inference to maximize performance on salient object detection for both monocular RGB and RGB-D images. By utilizing data augmentation that incorporates salient objects from the other modality during training, the network learns to effectively handle images of both types. During inference, the network is asked to predict three distinct output channels corresponding to the foreground, background, and depth masks. These masks are then combined through element-wise multiplication to achieve salient object detection on images with or without depth information. Comprehensive experiments were conducted to validate the efficacy of the proposed framework, and results indicate significant improvements in accuracy.

The UM-IU@LING system for the SemEval-2019 task on detecting aggression in social media posts is composed of two primary models, each with a different approach to sub-tasks. The first model, responsible for broad aggression class prediction, leverages BERT as a state-of-the-art language model and incorporates multi-task learning to enhance its performance. The second model, a set of four SVM classifiers, predicts the specific categories of aggression. Its input is derived from BERT's final layer, and it was fine-tuned using both training and validation datasets to optimize feature representation.

A number is considered a palindrome if its decimal representation reads the same forward and backward, such as $121 = \overline{121}$. This paper explores the multiplicative quorients $\frac{ab}{\overline{ba}}$, where $a$ and $b$ are palindromic or non-pindromic numbers with no prime factors in common and $a > b > 1$. In the case of non-palindromic numbers, the set of valid values for the quotient is shown to be infinite. However, if both numbers are palindromic, the valid values for the quotient are restricted to a finite set of values, specifically $\{2, 3, 5, 7, 11\}$.

Computed Tomography (CT) is widely employed in various fields, including medical diagnostics and industrial inspections. To enhance its performance, reconstruction methods have been developed that combine the advantages of iterative techniques and reconstruction algorithms. Our novel approach polyenergetic CT reconstruction, denoising and material decomposition (PCTDm) integrates a reconstruction algorithm into the CT inverse problem as a regularisation term in the associated variational model. Based on an energy function that accounts for observation, information, regularisation and material terms, our model simultaneously performs CT reconstruction, removal of CT image noise and material decomposition. We demonstrate its effectiveness on synthetic polyenergetic CT reconstruction tasks using 2D and 3D simulations of different imaging setups, different levels of noise and different types of materials. Our model shows that a suitable material term can be designed to improve both information and material fidelity, and that various information terms enable ct reconstruction and material decomposition while preserving different properties of the estimated image.

Handwritten Text Recognition (HTR) models trained on limited data suffer from data scarcity issues. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel data creation approach. By leveraging pre-trained neural networks, we generate diverse training samples from a single reference document. The proposed method involves three key components: (1) generating realistic image data with varied styles and content, (1b) producing synthetic data given a reference image, (2) c) creating reference images from known data. The proposed approach yields improved training results, achieving comparable performance to models trained on extensive datasets of historical documents. Additionally, it has a notable advantage in significantly reducing the processing time and memory requirements.

Researchers have developed a novel merging technique to integrate heavy nucleus calculations performed within the ab initio no-core shell model. This approach enables the simultaneous description of multiple heavy nuclei, utilizing a unified, adequately large shell model diagonalization. It's anticipated that this method will be a valuable tool for analyzing the properties of various naturally occurring and synthetic heavy nuclei. To demonstrate its efficacy, the method has been applied to calculations of $^{110}$Cd nucleus, with particularly nice results.

We begin to understand the SSH model from a student's perspective, incorporating historical context and experimental developments. Mathematical descriptions are accompanied by discussions of the physical significance of key parameters. Topological invariants and their relationships to other models are explained, alongside the impact of interactions and disorder on topological properties. Finally, we examine edge modes in finite systems and their connection to topological invariant boundary state polynomial, as well as the potential applications of these modes in generating entangled states.

This study examines the compactness of composition operators within Bergman spaces associated with specific types of domains in complex space, specifically those resulting from the boundary type of any convex region, as well as Stein domains that feature at least two non-bound homology groups. It then demonstrates that compactness of the composition operator with a given symbol $\varphi$ within these Bergman spaces necessitates the operator being continuous, a requirement that is fulfilled only when $\varphi$ meets certain criteria involving compact regions in complex space, or analytic discs with specific properties. This result is applicable across the full Bergman spaces and their semi-continuous variants for strictly convex domains, leading to a characterization of $C^2$ mappings that preserve strict convexity, or more generally, convexity, when considering their effect on Bergman spaces and their semi-continuous variants.

We employ a two-step quantization approach to compute two-loop amplitudes in supergravity on the background of AdS5xS5 with various scalar, fermionic, and vector particle contents. By applying the Witten-equivalence principle, these amplitudes can be expressed in terms of vector theories on a 6-dimensional manifold derived from the superspace of the super Yang-Mills theory on a 4-dimensional sphere through the AdS5xR approach. As a result, our findings confirm the finiteness of N=8 supergravity on the background of AdS5 with positive cosmological constant, with the divergence at two loops matching the prediction from the Kolmog Zenkov beta function.

High-performance programming on GPUs is challenging, especially when it comes to memory management, as the GPU's high memory bandwidth can be hampered by misaligned or irregular memory access patterns. This issue is particularly pronounced when using memory allocators, which are crucial for simplifying memory management and boosting performance in high-performance CPU applications, including object-based programming languages like Java and Python. Despite the availability of custom GPU memory allocators, they have limitations when it comes to handling object-based programming, which involves diverse memory access patterns due to varying memory alignments, access sizes, and pointer arithmetic. As a result, existing GPU memory allocators have failed to deliver optimal performance in GPU object-based programming, which relies heavily on custom object allocation but struggles with mixed memory access patterns. To overcome this challenge, a new GPU memory allocator called DynaSOAr has been developed, specifically designed for mixed memory access patterns and object-based GPU programming. DynaSOAr is a fine-grained, lock-free GPU memory allocator that uses an improved version of hash table to minimize memory conflicts and optimize access patterns, including unified memory management that minimizes the impact of misaligned and irregular memory access patterns. Comprehensive evaluations have shown that DynaSOAr is up to 2.15 times faster than the current best GPU memory allocators and 1.55 times faster than CPU memory allocators in real-world GPU object-based programming workloads, with nearly negligible overhead for correct operation.

In many situations, traditional and modern machine learning approaches may be susceptible to adversarial attacks, which can exploit their inherent vulnerabilities. To address this limitation, we introduce a method for computing assurance regions in the context of credal Bayesian networks, which provide robust guarantees against interference, akin to the concept of influence regions in classification models. By representing a credal network as a probabilistic model, and formulating the assurance region calculation as an optimization problem over its structure, we employ a cutting-plane relaxation, and devise an efficient algorithm to achieve convergence and optimality. We compare our approach to state-of-the-art methods in terms of accuracy, efficiency, and attack vector quality, and test it on diverse real-world datasets, such as the FLIGHT model, and large-scale data from the NASA flight data repository, showing our approach outperforms existing techniques.

Researchers have created a innovative, acoustically manipulated ultrasonic beam steering system that utilizes a phased array and a standing sound wave to manipulate a separate, moving beam.  By altering the effective properties of the beam's path within the standing wave pattern, it is possible to control its direction of propagation, even if the system is not designed to typically do so.  To facilitate this manipulation, a new ultrasonic generator has been developed to accurately and dynamically control the phase of the array.  To demonstrate the system's capabilities, air-borne ultrasonic waves have been successfully manipulated using this innovative technique.

A vector code is considered neighbour-transitive if the same number of neighbours is shared by all code words, and its words distances form a specific triplet of values. In this study, we examine neighbour-transitive codes within the framework of generalised quadrangles, particularly those defined in a general quadrangle $\Gamma$. The first line of investigation focuses on code lengths for such codes, and a partial spread definition is introduced in this context. Theorems are developed to establish upper limits on code lengths for 1- and 2- neighbour-transitive codes containing lines from $\Gamma$, as well as those containing points or lines. Moreover, we examine the weights associated with neighbour-transitive codes whose code words define lines in $\Gamma$, and construct a set of such codes whose code words define points, alongside providing an outline for a proof that their weights are restricted to 1 and 2.

To quantify a quadratic form, $Q(a,b,c)$, in the anisotropic density framework, an anisotropic 2D correlation function has been proposed. This 2D correlation function is used to analyze molecular density in the CMZ by applying it to a $^{12}$CO ($J$ = 1--0) intensity map. This application helps compare various AZQ values and determine their significance in terms of anisotropy. A specific finding in the CMZ shows that CO intensity exhibits an elongated pattern, with an azimuthal variation amplitude of approximately 100% at scales of 100 pc, leading to CO column density variations of $\pm$20% in the $x$ direction and $\pm$40% in the $z$ direction.

To analyze electron interactions in solids, existing models like the two-component plasma model have been utilized with some success. A new model has been developed to investigate non-linear X-ray absorption spectra, taking into account groups of electrons excited by high-fluence X-ray pulses. This model employs a grid-based approach to solve Poisson's equation and has been validated using molecular dynamics for small systems and full simulations of large systems via X-ray photoemission calculations. The findings have been applied to non-linear X-ray absorption spectra of the element magnesium, and further research is planned on higher order spectra and other materials.

A low-power, area-efficient on-chip temperature sensor has been designed and fabricated in a 65nm CMOS process. Featuring a resolution of 0.24 degrees Celsius and an inaccuracy of within plus or minus 1.4 degrees Celsius, the detector operates over a temperature range of -10 to 70 degrees Celsius at supply voltages between 0.6V and 1.8V. Capable of completing a temperature measurement in under 10 microseconds, the detector consumes minimal energy, averaging around 1.06 nanojoules per measurement.

Quantum entanglement, a cornerstone of quantum information, is frequently diminished by environmental interference known as noise. This problem can be addressed by a strategy called noiseless amplification, or the quantum scissors, which amplifies a noisy state by extracting its most probable configuration and enhancing it to a pure state. In this study, we have developed an experimental approach to create polarization entanglement using this strategy. By precisely measuring the joint state of two photons and retaining only specific outcomes, we have successfully generated entangled photons. Our research has also included an assessment of the fidelity of the generated state, verifying its validity even when the final photons' detection is not predetermined.

We've optimized this for specific digit sets, given by specific Dreyfuss Driscoll Drechsler equations, yielding four-stretch, and provided a upper bound of O(kkks) for ss-skip multiskip multisets.
